"The sight of which might teach you what sort of enemies you have to war against, if you are a Christian, and how you may be sure to gain the victory. I see you, while the standard of salvation is in one hand, rushing on with a sword in the other, to the murder of your brother; and, under the banner of the cross, destroying the life of one who to the cross owes his salvation. The final paragraph of The Complaint of Peace finishes with the command 'resipiscite,' meaning a voluntary return from madness and unconsciousness:

'Consider, I beseech you, my complaints of the doctrines and morals of the Reformers, applying the same critique I had made about public Scholastic disputations: Look around on this 'Evangelical' generation, and observe whether amongst them less indulgence is given to luxury, lust, or avarice, than amongst those whom you so detest. Show me any one person who by that Gospel has been reclaimed from drunkenness to sobriety, from fury and passion to meekness, from avarice to liberality, from reviling to well-speaking, from wantonness to modesty.'"

This passage is a critique of the Reformers and their followers, urging them to reflect on their actions and the impact of their teachings. The speaker accuses them of waging war against their own brothers and sisters, while claiming to uphold the banner of the cross. The speaker challenges the Reformers to show evidence of the positive effects of their teachings on people's behavior and morals. The passage ends with the Latin word "resipiscite," which means "come to your senses" or "return to a sound mind," emphasizing the need for self-reflection and change.
